title: Twitter and Facebook posts about COVID-19 are less likely to spread misinformation compared to other health topics
screen_reason: About 325 million Twitter and Facebook posts sharing URLs (8 March - 1 May 2020 vs the same window in 2019) were classified by source credibility, and a stratified random sample of 3,000 COVID-19 posts was human-coded for misinformation. The human-coded misinformation shares are stated verbatim with confidence intervals for four strata (more credible 5.33%, less credible 8.50%, unrated 7.33%, in-platform 5.17%; n = 600 each), each an item-level falsity share with an explicit denominator. The study's headline source-credibility proportions are reported only as rate ratios and in figures, so they yield no rows.

estimates.platform: Twitter, Facebook Pages and Facebook Groups (200 sampled posts from each of the three COVID-19 datasets)
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19 posts linking to 'more credible' sources that human annotators coded as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 600 COVID-19 posts linking to 'more credible' top-level domains (200 randomly selected from each of the Twitter, Facebook Pages and Facebook Groups COVID-19 datasets), part of a stratified sample of 3,000 posts
estimates.definition: Annotator coded the post 'Misinformation = Yes' if the message contains egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19, including news reports repeating such claims or any story promoting misinformation
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation Yes = if the message contains egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19. Also, news reports repeating these claims. Any story that is promoting misinformation."
estimates.source_quote: when compared to “more credible” sources (5.33% misinformation, 95% CI: 3.41–7.26, n = 600).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Content of credibility categories', pp. 5-6; Fig 1; S2 Fig caption
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three authors (DK, FF, AMJ) hand-coded batches of 100 posts per platform against a written codebook until Krippendorff's alpha > 0.80 (alpha1 = 0.742, then alpha2 = 0.811); disagreements resolved by majority with ties adjudicated by a fourth author (DAB); the remaining 2,400 posts were split at random between the three annotators. The credibility STRATA themselves come from third-party domain lists (NewsGuard and MediaBiasFactCheck, r = 0.81, averaged where both available), but the misinformation label on each row is human coding.
estimates.moderator_quote: We generated a stratified sample of 3000 posts by randomly selecting 200 posts from each COVID-19 dataset for each credibility category (More, Less, Not Credible, Unrated) and a set of 200 "in platform" posts (i.e., those linking to Twitter from Twitter or Facebook from Facebook).
estimates.notes: NOT A POPULATION PREVALENCE: the sample is stratified by the credibility of the shared link with 200 posts per cell, so this and the sibling rows are stratum-conditional shares and must not be pooled or averaged without the population weights (which the paper does not print). CONSTRUCT CALL: coded CONTENT because the numerator is a truth judgement of the post's own message and the denominator is posts in the platforms' keyword streams; a SHARING/content_share reading is defensible since every sampled post shares a URL and the paper frames it as 'spreading misinformation' - hence borderline=true. breadth=misleading because the codebook includes 'misleading use of data' and news reports repeating claims. Within this stratum the paper also splits high-quality health sources (5.33%, 95% CI 0.00-10.42, n = 75) and other more credible traditional media (5.33%, 95% CI 3.41-7.26, n = 525); those sub-splits are not given separate rows.

estimates.platform: Twitter, Facebook Pages and Facebook Groups (200 sampled posts from each of the three COVID-19 datasets)
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19 posts linking to 'less credible' sources that human annotators coded as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 600 COVID-19 posts linking to 'less credible' top-level domains (200 randomly selected from each of the Twitter, Facebook Pages and Facebook Groups COVID-19 datasets)
estimates.definition: Annotator coded the post 'Misinformation = Yes' (egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19); 'less credible' = top-level domain rated 33-67% by NewsGuard, or 'mostly factual' (60%) or 'mixed' (40%) on the MediaBiasFactCheck factual-reporting scale
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation Yes = if the message contains egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19. Also, news reports repeating these claims. Any story that is promoting misinformation."

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three trained annotators, codebook-based, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.811 on the second round, majority resolution with a fourth author adjudicating ties; stratum membership from NewsGuard / MediaBiasFactCheck domain ratings.
estimates.moderator_quote: Top-level domains were considered "less credible" if they were given a credibility rating between 33% and 67% by NewsGuard, or rated as "mostly factual" (60%) or "mixed" (40%) on the MediaBiasFactCheck factual reporting scale
estimates.notes: Stratum-conditional share from the same 3,000-post stratified sample; n = 600 per category is stated in the S2 Fig caption ('n = 600 for each credibility category') and follows from 200 posts x 3 COVID-19 datasets. Do not pool with the sibling rows.

estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19 posts linking to 'unrated' sources (domains with no NewsGuard/MediaBiasFactCheck rating) that human annotators coded as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 600 COVID-19 posts linking to top-level domains that had no credibility rating (200 randomly selected from each of the Twitter, Facebook Pages and Facebook Groups COVID-19 datasets)
estimates.definition: Annotator coded the post 'Misinformation = Yes' (egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19); 'unrated' = shared top-level domain absent from both NewsGuard and MediaBiasFactCheck (only 2.6% of the 554,378 unique domains, though 47% of all URLs, were rated)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation Yes = if the message contains egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19. Also, news reports repeating these claims. Any story that is promoting misinformation."
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Content of credibility categories', p. 6; Fig 1; S3 Fig
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three trained annotators, codebook-based, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.811 on the second round, majority resolution with a fourth author adjudicating ties; the stratum is defined by the ABSENCE of a third-party domain rating.
estimates.moderator_quote: 14,609 (2.6%) of these unique top-level domains were assigned a credibility rating, these top-level domains accounted for 19,294,621 (47%) of all URLs shared. The remaining URLs were unrated
estimates.notes: Useful stratum because unrated domains are about half of all shared URLs; the authors use this figure to argue the unrated half was 'not primarily misinformative'. Stratum-conditional: do not pool with the sibling rows.

estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19 posts whose links stayed 'in platform' (Twitter to Twitter, Facebook to Facebook) that human annotators coded as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 600 COVID-19 posts whose URLs pointed back into the same platform (200 randomly selected from each of the Twitter, Facebook Pages and Facebook Groups COVID-19 datasets)
estimates.definition: Annotator coded the post 'Misinformation = Yes' (egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19); 'in platform' = posts linking to Twitter from Twitter or to Facebook from Facebook
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation Yes = if the message contains egregious falsehoods, conspiracy theories, or misleading use of data related to COVID-19. Also, news reports repeating these claims. Any story that is promoting misinformation."

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three trained annotators, codebook-based, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.811 on the second round, majority resolution with a fourth author adjudicating ties; this stratum has no third-party source rating at all (self-referential links).
estimates.moderator_quote: and a set of 200 "in platform" posts (i.e., those linking to Twitter from Twitter or Facebook from Facebook)
estimates.notes: Stratum-conditional share. 'In platform' is not a credibility grade but a residual category of self-referential links, which is why it is the closest thing in this paper to an unfiltered social-media post sample; still not a population prevalence. Do not pool with the sibling rows.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) THE 'NOT CREDIBLE' STRATUM'S MISINFORMATION SHARE IS NOT EXTRACTABLE: the text gives only the risk ratio ('those with URLs rated as "not credible" were 3.67 (95% CI: 3.50-3.71) times more likely to contain false claims than "more credible" sources') and puts the proportion in Fig 1 only. Multiplying 3.67 x 5.33% would be a computed value, forbidden by R8, so no row. (2) THE STUDY'S HEADLINE CREDIBILITY SHARES ARE FIGURE-ONLY: the proportions of COVID-19 vs 2019-health URLs in each credibility category are shown in Fig 2 with no numbers in the text; only rate ratios are printed (not credible: Twitter RR = 0.37, Facebook Pages RR = 0.41, Facebook Groups RR = 0.37; more credible: RR = 1.13 / 1.07 / 1.03; high-quality health sources RR = 3.52 / 1.15 / 1.09; unrated RR = 0.67 / 0.74 / 0.58). Ratios are not shares, so no SHARING/CONTENT rows for the source-credibility measure - which is the paper's main analysis. This means the extraction under-represents the study. (3) Sub-splits of the 'more credible' stratum (high-quality government/academic health sources 5.33%, 95% CI 0.00-10.42, n = 75; other more credible traditional media 5.33%, 95% CI 3.41-7.26, n = 525) were not given rows as sub-subgroups of an already stratum-conditional cell. (4) The 2019 'other health topics' comparison datasets have no printed human-coded misinformation shares (the 3,000-post annotation sample was drawn from the COVID-19 datasets only), so no pre-pandemic row and no country/topic contrast row. (5) Corpus descriptors (305,129,859 Twitter posts; 13,437,700 Facebook page posts; 6,577,307 Facebook group posts; 41,134,540 URLs; 554,378 unique domains; 14,609 (2.6%) rated domains covering 19,294,621 (47%) of URLs) are volumes/coverage, not misinformation shares. (6) Virality results (negative binomial regressions, Fig 3) are engagement, not exposure shares. (7) The three platforms' 200-post-per-cell samples are pooled into each n = 600 row; per-platform misinformation shares are not printed, so no platform split was possible even though the review would normally split by platform.

rob.design: Very large-scale observational design: all public English-language Twitter posts matching #Coronavirus/#CoronaOutbreak/#COVID19 (8 Mar - 1 May 2020) via the streaming API plus CrowdTangle Facebook Pages (>100,000 likes) and Groups (>=95,000 members, or US-based with >=2,000), against the same dates in 2019 with generalised health keywords; misinformation proxied at scale by top-level-domain credibility from NewsGuard and MediaBiasFactCheck (r = 0.81), validated on a stratified random sample of 3,000 posts hand-coded by three authors to Krippendorff's alpha = 0.811 with majority resolution and fourth-author tie-breaking; roughly half of shared URLs were unrated; keyword-based inclusion may add noise; IRB-exempt public data.
